entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen29949" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29950" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29951" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29951" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29950" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29952" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains a summary of the judgments denounced by Jeremiah against Judah, Babylon, and many other nations. It begins with reproving the Jews for disobeying the calls of God to repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.1-Jer.25.7">Jer 25:1-7</reference>; on which account their captivity, with that of her neighboring nations, during seventy years, is foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.8-Jer.25.11">Jer 25:8-11</reference>. At the expiration of that period, (computing from the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, to the famous edict of the first year of Cyrus), an end was to be put to the Babylonian empire, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12-Jer.25.14">Jer 25:12-14</reference>. All this is again declared by the emblem of that cup of wrath which the prophet, as it should seem in a vision, tendered to all the nations which he enumerates, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.29">Jer 25:15-29</reference>. And for farther confirmation, it is a third time repeated in a very beautiful and elevated strain of poetry, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30-Jer.25.38">Jer 25:30-38</reference>. The talent of diversifying the ideas, images, and language, even when the subject is the same, or nearly so, appears no where in such perfection as among the sacred poets. <div eID="gen29952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29953" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29954" type="x-p"/> The word that came to Jeremiah - to the fourth year - This prophecy, we see, was delivered in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and the chapter that contains it is utterly out of its place. It should be between chapters 35 and 36. <div eID="gen29954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29955" type="x-p"/> The defeat of the Egyptians by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, and the subsequent taking of Jerusalem, occurred in this year, viz., the fourth year of Jehoiakim. <div eID="gen29955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29956" type="x-p"/> The first year of Nebuchadrezzar - This king was associated with his father two years before the death of the latter. The Jews reckon his reign from this time, and this was the first of those two years; but the Chaldeans date the commencement of his reign two years later, viz., at the death of his father.
entries.content_plain: Introduction This chapter contains a summary of the judgments denounced by Jeremiah against Judah, Babylon, and many other nations. It begins with reproving the Jews for disobeying the calls of God to repentance, Jer 25:1-7 ; on which account their captivity, with that of her neighboring nations, during seventy years, is foretold, Jer 25:8-11 . At the expiration of that period, (computing from the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, to the famous edict of the first year of Cyrus), an end was to be put to the Babylonian empire, Jer 25:12-14 . All this is again declared by the emblem of that cup of wrath which the prophet, as it should seem in a vision, tendered to all the nations which he enumerates, Jer 25:15-29 . And for farther confirmation, it is a third time repeated in a very beautiful and elevated strain of poetry, Jer 25:30-38 . The talent of diversifying the ideas, images, and language, even when the subject is the same, or nearly so, appears no where in such perfection as among the sacred poets. Verse 1 The word that came to Jeremiah - to the fourth year - This prophecy, we see, was delivered in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and the chapter that contains it is utterly out of its place. It should be between chapters 35 and 36. The defeat of the Egyptians by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, and the subsequent taking of Jerusalem, occurred in this year, viz., the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The first year of Nebuchadrezzar - This king was associated with his father two years before the death of the latter. The Jews reckon his reign from this time, and this was the first of those two years; but the Chaldeans date the commencement of his reign two years later, viz., at the death of his father.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29960" type="x-p"/> I will take from them - See <reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">Jer 7:34</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.9">Jer 16:9</reference>. <div eID="gen29960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29961" type="x-p"/> The sound of the mill-stones, and the light of the candle - These two are conjoined, because they generally ground the corn before day, by the light of the candle. Sir J. Chardin has remarked, that every where in the morning may be heard the noise of the mills; for they generally grind every day just as much as is necessary for the day's consumption. Where then the noise of the grill is not heard, nor the light of the candle seen, there must be desolation; because these things are heard and seen in every inhabited country.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29962" type="x-p"/> Shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years - As this prophecy was delivered in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and in the first of Nebuchadnezzar, and began to be accomplished in the same year, (for then Nebuchadnezzar invaded Judea, and took Jerusalem), seventy years from this time will reach down to the first year of Cyrus, when he made his proclamation for the restoration of the Jews, and the rebuilding of Jerusalem. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Isa 13:19</reference> (note), where the subject is farther considered in relation to the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, and the city of Babylon.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29967" type="x-p"/> Then took I the cup - and made all the nations to drink - This cup of God's wrath is merely symbolical, and simply means that the prophet should declare to all these people that they shall fall under the Chaldean yoke, and that this is a punishment inflicted on them by God for their iniquities. "Then I took the cup;" I declared publicly the tribulation that God was about to bring on Jerusalem, the cities of Judah, and all the nations.

navigation_sections.content_plain: Introduction This chapter contains a summary of the judgments denounced by Jeremiah against Judah, Babylon, and many other nations. It begins with reproving the Jews for disobeying the calls of God to repentance, Jer 25:1-7 ; on which account their captivity, with that of her neighboring nations, during seventy years, is foretold, Jer 25:8-11 . At the expiration of that period, (computing from the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, to the famous edict of the first year of Cyrus), an end was to be put to the Babylonian empire, Jer 25:12-14 . All this is again declared by the emblem of that cup of wrath which the prophet, as it should seem in a vision, tendered to all the nations which he enumerates, Jer 25:15-29 . And for farther confirmation, it is a third time repeated in a very beautiful and elevated strain of poetry, Jer 25:30-38 . The talent of diversifying the ideas, images, and language, even when the subject is the same, or nearly so, appears no where in such perfection as among the sacred poets.

It begins with reproving the Jews for disobeying the calls of God to repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.1-Jer.25.7">Jer 25:1-7</reference>; on which account their captivity, with that of her neighboring nations, during seventy years, is foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.8-Jer.25.11">Jer 25:8-11</reference>. At the expiration of that period, (computing from the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, to the famous edict of the first year of Cyrus), an end was to be put to the Babylonian empire, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12-Jer.25.14">Jer 25:12-14</reference>. All this is again declared by the emblem of that cup of wrath which the prophet, as it should seem in a vision, tendered to all the nations which he enumerates, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.29">Jer 25:15-29</reference>. And for farther confirmation, it is a third time repeated in a very beautiful and elevated strain of poetry, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30-Jer.25.38">Jer 25:30-38</reference>. The talent of diversifying the ideas, images, and language, even when the subject is the same, or nearly so, appears no where in such perfection as among the sacred poets. <div eID="gen29952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29953" type="x-p"/>
